messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims, Loss Themes: Talk about people loosing loved ones
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Weakness Belief: I am a weak person, Dehumanization: I feel like an object, not like a person, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

John, a 55-year-old man of Oceania descent, has been working as a nanny for several years, helping to care for children in various households. His life took a dramatic turn when he witnessed the traumatic event that left an indelible mark on his psyche—a tragic accident involving one of the children under his care. It was a sunny afternoon, and John had taken three young boys to play at a local park. The eldest boy, Tommy, who was only 10 years old, had fallen from the jungle gym and hit his head on the concrete below. Despite John’s immediate efforts to call for help and administer first aid, Tommy succumbed to his injuries before an ambulance arrived. Since that fateful day, John has found himself unable to shake off the haunting memories of the event. He often feels triggered by visual cues such as seeing children playing in playgrounds or even specific body parts associated with the injury—like a child’s head or face. These triggers have led him to avoid parks and other places where he might encounter similar scenes. John struggles intensely when talking about what happened, often losing his train of thought and unable to explain clearly what transpired that day. When memories flood back, he hears in his mind the sounds of the accident—the fall from the jungle gym, Tommy's cries for help, and the frantic calls for an ambulance. These auditory recollections are accompanied by overwhelming grief each time John recalls the event. His self-perception has also been profoundly affected. John has come to believe that he is a weak person, incapable of handling such a situation effectively. He feels like an object rather than a human being, his sense of worth eroded by the belief that he failed to protect Tommy and should have done more to prevent the tragedy. John’s daily life as a nanny has been significantly impacted by these symptoms. He avoids taking children out for activities where they might be exposed to playgrounds or any environment reminiscent of the traumatic event. This avoidance has led to strained relationships with his employers, who perceive him as overly cautious and perhaps even neglectful in his duties. John’s sense of self-worth has diminished further due to his belief that he should have protected Tommy more effectively. He feels like a failure, not only for losing a child under his care but also for feeling unable to explain the incident clearly without breaking down emotionally. His grief is compounded by the loss themes he encounters in conversations with other parents or caretakers who talk about their own fears and experiences of losing loved ones. Despite these struggles, John has never before sought help, believing that it was a sign of weakness to do so. However, his symptoms have become increasingly debilitating, affecting both his personal life and work performance. The constant triggers and grief are overwhelming, and he is no longer able to function effectively in his role as a nanny. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could not continue living with these intense emotions and fears. He is most afraid of being seen as inadequate or weak by others, but at the same time, he hopes for support and validation that would allow him to regain some sense of self-worth and strength. He seeks understanding and guidance on how to navigate his grief and the traumatic memories without feeling like a failure.
